title: Two Roads
sum: Psalm 1 is the doorway into the Psalter. It has no title, no prayer and no music direction. It describes the happy person who will not take the advice of the wicked, linger on the sinners' road or sit with the mockers, but who delights in the LORD's teaching and murmurs over it day and night. That person is a tree set out by water channels, green and fruitful; the wicked are husks blown off the threshing floor. The last verse sums it up: the LORD knows the road of the righteous, and the road of the wicked will be lost.

Placed first, the psalm tells the reader how to use the book: the Psalms are torah, instruction, to be read and repeated, not only sung. With Psalm 2 it forms a double introduction, framed by "Happy" (1:1; 2:12). In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 1.
readings: Psalm 1 sounds like Proverbs: two ways, two outcomes, a tree and chaff. Many scholars count it among the wisdom or torah psalms (with 19 and 119), written by teachers who shaped Israel's prayer book after the exile so that it would form readers in the way of the LORD's teaching.

Christian tradition from Jerome and Augustine read the "happy man" as Christ, the one person who never walked in the advice of the wicked, and the tree as the cross or the tree of life. Jewish tradition read him as the student of Torah, who repeats God's teaching until it becomes his own.

views.H: An ancient teaching psalm with no author named; some Jewish tradition ascribed it with Psalm 2 to David as one psalm (Bavli Berakhot 9b), and others to Ezra or the collectors of the book.
views.C: A late wisdom or torah psalm, probably written or placed here by the editors of the Psalter in the Persian or early Greek period. Its vocabulary is close to Proverbs, Jeremiah 17:5–8 and Joshua 1:8, and its purpose is to frame the whole book as instruction.
views.L: Psalm 1 is sung on many feasts and at the start of the weekly cycle of psalms in monastic prayer. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it opens the four-week psalter at Sunday Office of Readings. In Jewish custom the Psalter is often read through in a week or a month, beginning with Psalm 1.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms begins by comparing the five books of the Psalter with the five books of Moses. Rabbis read 1:1 as a ladder of sin and 1:2 as a call to study Torah day and night; the Talmud says one should study what one's heart desires, since "his delight is in the law" (Bavli Avodah Zarah 19a).
views.X: The fathers often read the psalm of Christ the righteous man and of the baptized believer planted by the water of the Spirit. Luther called Psalm 1 the preface to the whole Psalter and read the "law" as God's word in law and gospel.

echoes: Jeremiah 17:5–8; Joshua 1:8; Proverbs 4:14–19; Psalm 19:7–11; Psalm 112:1; Psalm 119:1–3; Matthew 7:13–14; Matthew 7:24–27; Revelation 22:2

settings.what: A teaching poem on the two ways
settings.to: Anyone who reads or hears the Psalter: the reader, not God, is addressed
settings.when: Placed at the head of the collection, probably by its editors after the exile; some think it once served as a teaching poem in wisdom circles
settings.why: To set before every reader the choice between two ways of life before the prayers begin, and to say that the book that follows is God's instruction to be taken in day and night. It promises that the life rooted in the LORD's teaching lasts, while the way of the wicked comes to nothing.
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, without a king and often under foreign rule, the psalm made the study of God's teaching the center of life, open to everyone, not only priests and kings.
views: Most scholars group it with Psalms 19 and 119 and with Proverbs: a product of Israel's teachers.
Childs, Wilson and others stress its place: it turns the Psalter into a book for reading and meditation, not only for temple singing.

deep.h: Which witnesses were checked for Psalms 1–17
deep.b:
Checked by the writer. The Hebrew of every verse in the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), through the site's Hebrew text and its word-by-word gloss, with the Ketiv and Qere readings it marks. The Old Greek in Rahlfs' edition and the Vulgate's Gallican Psalter, read for each of Psalms 1–17 on the sacred-texts.com polyglot pages (Greek 1–16, since Greek 9 covers Hebrew 9–10).

Cited as reported. The Aramaic Targum of Psalms (Stec's translation and the commentaries), Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus, the Syriac Peshitta and readings of medieval Hebrew manuscripts. These were not seen by the writer, and the notes say "as reported" where they are used.

The Dead Sea Scrolls. Five scrolls preserve parts of Psalms 1–17. Their contents below are taken, as reported, from the scroll-by-scroll listing of the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible translation site (dssenglishbible.com), which follows the official editions; they were not checked against Flint's list or the printed Dead Sea Scrolls Bible, and the fragments themselves were not seen. English verse numbers:

  • 4QPs-a (4Q83): 5:8–12; 6:1, 3, 5. At 5:9 the scroll begins the verse with a different word, of which only the first letter is legible.
  • 4QPs-c (4Q85): 16:6–10; 17:1. No difference is reported.
  • 8QPs (8Q2): 17:5–9, 14. No difference is reported.
  • 11QPs-c (11Q7): 2:1–8; 9:2–7; 12:4–8; 13:1–2, 4–5; 14:1–6; 17:9–15. At 17:9 it reads "seek" where the Masoretic Text has "ruined," and at 17:11 it lacks "our steps" and has other small differences.
  • The Nahal Hever Psalms scroll (5/6HevPs): parts of 7:12–16:1. At 15:3 the listing marks two phrases as missing; whether this is a real shorter text or damage could not be checked.

No scroll is reported to differ at the places debated in these notes: 2:12, 12:7, 14:3, 16:2 and 16:10 are either not preserved or agree with the Masoretic Text. A Qumran commentary, 4Q174 (the Florilegium), quotes 1:1 and 2:1–2 (as reported). Readers who want the readings should use Flint's study and the editions in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert.

title: The LORD's Anointed King
sum: The nations and their kings are in an uproar, plotting to throw off the rule of the LORD and his anointed king. In heaven the LORD laughs, then speaks in anger: he himself has set his king on Zion. The king then reports God's decree: "You are my son. This day I have fathered you." The nations are his inheritance; he will crush rebels like pottery. The psalm ends with a warning to the world's rulers to serve the LORD with fear, to "kiss the son" (2:12, a debated phrase), and with a blessing on all who shelter in him.

Psalm 2 is a royal psalm, most likely sung at the crowning of a king of David's line in Jerusalem. With Psalm 1 it opens the Psalter: the LORD's teaching and the LORD's king. The New Testament quotes it more than almost any other psalm, of Jesus' baptism, resurrection and reign. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 2.
readings: The king of Judah, newly anointed, faces restless vassal states. At his crowning a priest or prophet declares the LORD's decree, and the king is adopted as God's son, as 2 Samuel 7:14 promised. The world-wide claims are court language, the ideal of what the king of the LORD's choosing should be.

When Israel had no king, the psalm pointed forward. The Psalms of Solomon, a Qumran commentary (4Q174 quotes 2:1–2, as reported) and the rabbis read it of the Messiah son of David. The New Testament reads it of Jesus: the plot of the nations is the plot against him (Acts 4:25–28), the "this day" is his resurrection (Acts 13:33), and the iron rod is his final victory (Revelation 19:15).

views.H: Acts 4:25 names David as the author, and many readers take the psalm as David's, about his own anointing on Zion and the promise of 2 Samuel 7, speaking also as a prophet of his greater son.
views.C: A royal coronation psalm from the time of the kings of Judah (900s–500s BC), comparable with Egyptian and Assyrian enthronement texts in which a king is called the god's son and given a decree. Placed second by the editors to make the Psalter a book of hope in God's king.
views.L: In the Christian year Psalm 2 belongs to Christmas, the Epiphany and Easter; the Roman Office of Readings sings it on Christmas Day and the 1662 Book of Common Prayer appoints it for Easter morning. Handel's Messiah sets 2:1–4 and 2:9 just before the Hallelujah chorus.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 2:7–8 of the Messiah son of David (Bavli Sukkah 52a). Rashi notes that the rabbis read it of the Messiah, but that he prefers to read it of David, "as a reply to the heretics," that is, Christians; Radak reads the decree of David or the Messiah as chosen king, not as a son by nature.
views.X: The church fathers made 2:7 a key text of the Son's eternal generation, the "today" of eternity (Augustine). Hebrews 1:5 sets it beside 2 Samuel 7:14 to show the Son is greater than angels. The psalm's "kiss the son" became, for many Christian readers, a call to submit to Christ.

deep.h: How Jews and Christians read Psalm 2
deep.b:
Everyone agrees that the psalm first spoke of a king of David's line in Jerusalem. The question is what it means after that line ended in 586 BC. Jewish readers before Jesus already applied it to a future king: the Psalms of Solomon 17 and a scroll from Qumran (4Q174, the "Florilegium," as reported) join Psalm 2 with 2 Samuel 7. The rabbis kept this reading (Bavli Sukkah 52a), and medieval commentators were divided: Rashi says the rabbis applied it to the Messiah, but he himself reads it of David, partly to answer Christian claims; Ibn Ezra and Radak allow both David and the Messiah.

The New Testament reads the psalm of Jesus at three moments: his baptism (Mark 1:11), his resurrection (Acts 13:33) and his reign over the nations (Revelation 2:26–27; Revelation 19:15). Christians later made 2:7 a text about the eternal relation of Father and Son. Jewish interpreters answer that the psalm's "son" is adoption language for a human king, as 89:26–27 and 2 Samuel 7:14 show, and that its promises still await fulfillment. Both readings agree on the psalm's claim: the nations' rebellion will not stand against the king the LORD has chosen.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89:26–27; Psalm 110:1–2; Acts 4:25–28; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5; Mark 1:11; Revelation 2:26–27; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15

settings.by: The psalmist, then the LORD (2:6), then the king himself reporting the LORD's decree (2:7–9); Acts 4:25 credits David
settings.to: The rebellious nations and their rulers (2:1–3, 2:10–12); the king (2:7–9); in worship, the people of Jerusalem gathered for the crowning
settings.when: Most likely at the enthronement of a king of Judah on Zion, when subject peoples might test a new ruler; read later, after the kings, of the coming Messiah
settings.why: To declare that the new king rules by the LORD's own appointment, adopted as God's son, so that rebellion against him is rebellion against the LORD. For the king it is assurance; for the nations a warning and an invitation to submit and find shelter. Knowing the coronation setting explains the 'this day': it is the day of crowning, not the day of birth.
settings.readers: Judeans after the exile, with no king, sang it as a promise still open: God had not abandoned his anointed. Placed beside Psalm 1, it joined the hope for God's king to the daily study of God's teaching.
views: Most scholars (Gunkel, Mowinckel, Kraus) place it in a royal ritual in Jerusalem.
Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take it as a prophecy of the Messiah, spoken by David.
Others stress its role, with Psalm 1, as the editors' introduction to the book.

title: Morning in the Middle of Danger
sum: David, on the run from his son Absalom, counts his enemies: so many, and all saying God will not rescue him. But the LORD is his shield and his honor. He called, and the LORD answered from his holy mountain; he lay down, slept and woke, because the LORD held him. He will not fear ten thousand. He calls on God to rise up and strike, and ends: "Rescue is the LORD's!" with a blessing on the whole people.
Psalm 3 is the first psalm with a title and the first lament in the Psalter. Its mention of sleeping and waking made it a morning prayer. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 3.

views.H: The title places it during David's flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 15–17), perhaps the morning after the night by the Jordan (2 Samuel 17:22). The 'many' enemies and the taunt that God has abandoned him fit Shimei's curses (2 Samuel 16:7–8).
views.C: An individual lament, perhaps for a king or leader facing many enemies, possibly from the time of the monarchy. Most scholars think the title is an editor's link to Second Samuel, made by reading David's story beside the psalm (Childs).
views.L: In the Benedictine office Psalm 3 opened the night office (Vigils) every day (Rule of Benedict 9). In the Orthodox Church it is the first of the Six Psalms of Matins. It is widely used as a morning prayer.
views.J: The Talmud asks why a psalm about Absalom follows Psalm 2, about Gog and Magog, and answers that both concern rebellion against God's king (Bavli Berakhot 10a); it also notes (7b) that the title says 'psalm', not 'lament', because David was relieved that the rebel was his own son, who might show mercy.
views.X: Many fathers read 3:5 as Christ's death and resurrection: 'I lay down and slept; I rose, for the Lord upheld me.' Augustine reads the psalm three ways: of David, of Christ and of the church.

echoes: 2 Samuel 15:13–30; 2 Samuel 16:5–14; 2 Samuel 17:1–22; Psalm 4:8; Psalm 27:1–3; Matthew 27:43; Jonah 2:9

settings.by: David, according to the title; the voice of one leader beset by many enemies
settings.to: The LORD (3:1, 3:7), quoting the enemies (3:2); the last line blesses God's people
settings.when: The title: when David fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 15–17). Many scholars: any morning prayer of a king or person in danger, sung at the temple
settings.why: To bring a desperate situation to God, answer the enemies' claim that God has abandoned the psalmist, and stake everything on the LORD's rescue. The mention of sleep and waking gives a pattern of trust for anyone who lies down in danger.
settings.readers: The title invited later Israel to read the prayer with David's story, learning that even the king of Israel, betrayed by his own son, prayed his way through. The closing blessing turned it into a prayer for the whole people.
views: On the traditional view David composed it during or after his flight.
Most scholars think editors joined the psalm to 2 Samuel 15–17 later.

title: An Evening Prayer
sum: The psalmist asks God, who has given him room in tight places before, to answer again. He turns to people of standing who are damaging his honor and chasing what is empty and false: the LORD has chosen his loyal one and will hear. They should tremble and stop sinning, think it over on their beds, offer right sacrifices and trust the LORD. Many ask who will show them anything good; he prays for the light of God's face. His joy is greater than a bumper harvest, and he lies down in peace and sleeps at once.
Psalm 4 has long been an evening prayer, paired with Psalm 3 in the morning. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 4.

views.H: Traditional readers often place it, like Psalm 3, in the Absalom rebellion, with the 'men of standing' as Absalom's supporters.
views.C: A song of trust from an individual, perhaps a leader or a falsely accused person; some (Kraus) see a dispute with people who sought rain and harvest from other gods (4:2, 4:6–7).
views.L: Christian Compline (night prayer) has used Psalm 4 since early times: the Rule of Benedict sets it every night, and the Roman rite on Saturday evenings. Its last verse is a common bedtime prayer.
views.J: The verse 4:4 ('speak in your hearts on your beds') is read in the Talmud as advice to say the Shema at bedtime (Bavli Berakhot 4b–5a). Psalm 4:8 is echoed in the bedtime Shema prayers.
views.X: Paul quotes 4:4 (Greek) in Ephesians 4:26. Augustine describes in his Confessions (book 9) how reading Psalm 4 moved him after his conversion.

echoes: Psalm 3:5; Numbers 6:24–26; Ephesians 4:26; Deuteronomy 33:28; Proverbs 3:24; Psalm 31:8

settings.what: A prayer of trust at night
settings.by: David, according to the title; a person slandered by powerful people
settings.to: God (4:1, 4:6–8), and the 'men of standing' who oppose him (4:2–5)
settings.when: An evening, before sleep; perhaps in a time of drought or poor harvest (4:6–7); the title gives no event
settings.why: To ask God for a hearing, to warn the accusers to stop and think, and to show that peace comes from the LORD, not from full barns. It teaches trust that lets a person sleep.
settings.readers: Later Israel and the church made it a bedtime prayer, so that every hearer could end the day with the psalmist's peace.

title: Prayer at Daybreak
sum: At daybreak the psalmist lays out his plea before God, his King, and keeps watch for the answer. God takes no pleasure in evil; boasters, liars and the violent cannot stand before him. But the psalmist, by God's great loyal love, will enter his house and bow toward his holy temple. He asks God to lead him past his watching enemies, whose mouths are open graves, to hold them guilty and thrust them out, and to cover all who shelter in him with favor like a great shield.
Psalm 5 is a morning prayer of someone falsely accused who comes to the sanctuary. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 5.

views.H: A prayer of David; traditional readers sometimes place it in the time of Absalom or of Saul's persecution. The mention of the temple suggests to some that David wrote for the sanctuary he planned.
views.C: An individual lament of an accused person seeking asylum and justice in the temple at the morning hour, probably from the time of the monarchy or later.
views.L: Psalm 5 was a morning psalm in many monastic orders, and in the Roman rite it is sung at Morning Prayer on Monday of the first week. 5:7 ("by the greatness of your loyal love I will enter your house") opens the Jewish morning service in many prayer books (Mah Tovu).
views.J: The verse 5:7 is said on entering the synagogue, joined with Numbers 24:5 ('How good are your tents, Jacob') in the Mah Tovu prayer.
views.X: Paul quotes 5:9 in Romans 3:13. The fathers read the psalm as the church's prayer at dawn, and 'my King and my God' was applied to Christ.

echoes: Romans 3:13; Psalm 15:1; Psalm 88:13; Psalm 143:8; Numbers 24:5; Habakkuk 2:1

settings.what: A morning prayer for protection and justice
settings.by: David, according to the title; a worshiper falsely accused by liars
settings.when: At daybreak, the hour of the morning offering and of judgment (5:3), as he comes to the sanctuary
settings.why: To set his case before God, to claim access to God's house by God's loyal love, not by merit, and to ask God to judge the liars. It assures all who shelter in God of his protection.
settings.readers: For later worshipers the psalm became a prayer on entering the house of God, and a reminder that only loyal love opens its doors.

title: Do Not Rebuke Me in Your Anger
sum: A sick and frightened man begs the LORD not to discipline him in anger. His bones and his soul are in terror; he has worn himself out groaning, soaking his bed with tears night after night. He asks God to come back and save him for the sake of his loyal love, because in Sheol no one gives God thanks. Then the mood turns at once: he orders the evildoers away, for the LORD has heard his weeping and will receive his prayer.
Christian tradition counts Psalm 6 as the first of seven penitential psalms. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 6.

views.H: A prayer of David in sickness or distress; some traditions link it with his illness or his grief after his sin with Bathsheba.
views.C: An individual lament of a sick person, who sees illness as God's discipline and fears death. The sudden turn at 6:8 suggests an answer was received, perhaps a priest's oracle.
views.L: One of the seven penitential psalms of Christian tradition (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), long prayed in Lent; in Judaism it is part of the Ashkenazi weekday Tachanun prayers.
views.J: One midrash reads 'on the sheminith', 'the eighth', of circumcision on the eighth day. In Tachanun it is said with the head resting on the arm, a posture of grief.
views.X: The fathers read 'the eighth' as the day of judgment and resurrection. Luther's first published book (1517) was on the seven penitential psalms. Jesus' 'Get away from me' (Matthew 7:23) quotes 6:8.

echoes: Psalm 38:1; Jeremiah 10:24; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 88:10–12; Isaiah 38:18–19; Matthew 7:23; Luke 13:27; John 12:27; Hebrews 12:5–11

traditions.q: What does "For among the dead no one calls you to mind" (6:5) say about the state of the dead?
views: The verse speaks of the dead from the viewpoint of this life and of the old covenant's limited knowledge. Since Christ's death the souls of the faithful are with God or being purified, and can be prayed for and can pray (Catechism 958, 1030–1032).
Before Christ the dead were held in Hades; Christ descended and opened it. The departed are alive in God, and the church prays for them, especially at memorial services where psalms are sung.

The psalm voices the terror of death under God's anger; the dead in Christ rest with him. Lutherans reject purgatory and Masses for the dead; the Apology of the Augsburg Confession (24) does not forbid prayers for the dead, and Lutheran funeral rites commend the departed to God.
The souls of believers at death are made perfect and pass into glory; the verse means the dead can no longer praise God among the living on earth (Westminster Confession 32.1).
The dead are unconscious, sleeping until the resurrection; 6:5, with Ecclesiastes 9:5 and Psalm 115:17, is read as plain teaching on this (Fundamental Beliefs 26).
The dead are not conscious and do not exist as souls apart from the body; Sheol is the common grave of mankind, and hope rests in the resurrection.

settings.by: David, according to the title; a man seriously ill and mocked by enemies
settings.when: During a severe illness, perhaps at the sanctuary; the change at 6:8 may follow a word of assurance
settings.why: To plead for healing and mercy from the God whose discipline he fears, to argue that his death would end his praise, and then to declare that his prayer has been heard. It gave the sick words for both terror and hope.
settings.readers: Israel prayed it in sickness and grief; the church made it a prayer of repentance, though the psalm itself never names a sin.
views: Most scholars read it as a prayer in illness (6:2).
Christian tradition reads the rebuke and discipline as signs of sin, and prays it in repentance.

title: The Innocent Man's Oath
sum: Hunted by an enemy who will tear him like a lion, the psalmist swears his innocence: if he has done this wrong, let the enemy trample him into the dust. He calls on the LORD to rise in anger, to take his seat as judge over the gathered nations, and to judge him by his innocence. God tests hearts and minds and is angry at evil every day. The wicked man sharpens his sword, conceives trouble, digs a pit and falls into it; his violence lands on his own head. The psalm ends in thanks to the LORD Most High.
Psalm 7 is a prayer of the falsely accused, with an oath of innocence. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 7.

views.H: The title links it with 'Cush, a Benjaminite', probably one of Saul's men slandering David (1 Samuel 24:9; 26:19); the Talmud and Targum take Cush as Saul himself.
views.C: An individual lament with a judicial oath, perhaps used in a temple procedure for an accused person (1 Kings 8:31–32). The title is an editor's link to David's conflicts with Saul's house.
views.L: Used in the church's daily office as a prayer for justice, and by individuals facing false accusation.
views.J: The Talmud (Moed Katan 16b) reads 'Cush' as Saul, 'different in his deeds as a Cushite is in his skin.'
views.X: Augustine, following the Greek 'Chousi', took Cush as Hushai, David's friend who deceived Absalom (2 Samuel 15:32–37), and read the psalm also as the prayer of Christ against his betrayer. Many Christians read the pit image as the cross, where evil fell into its own trap.

echoes: 1 Samuel 24:9–15; 1 Samuel 26:19; 2 Samuel 16:5–8; 1 Kings 8:31–32; Job 31:5–40; Psalm 9:15–16; Proverbs 26:27; Esther 7:10; James 1:15

settings.what: A prayer of an accused man, with an oath
settings.by: David, according to the title; a person falsely accused
settings.to: The LORD (7:1–9, 7:17); 7:10–16 speak about God and the wicked
settings.when: The title: 'about the words of Cush, a Benjaminite', a slander from Saul's tribe. Many scholars: an accused person's appeal at the sanctuary when no human court could decide
settings.why: To swear innocence before God, invite God's judgment on himself if he lies, and ask the judge of the nations to act. It teaches that evil plans fall back on those who make them.
settings.readers: Later Israel learned to bring false charges to God's court and to trust that God, who judges nations, hears an individual's case.

title: What Are Humans?
sum: Psalm 8 begins and ends with the same cry: "LORD, our Lord, how mighty your name is through all the earth!" Between those lines the psalmist looks at the night sky, the work of God's fingers, and asks why God should care about mere mortals. Yet God has made humans only a little less than God, crowned them with glory and set them over all creatures, flocks and herds, wild animals, birds and fish. Even the voices of babies are God's defense against his enemies.
Psalm 8 is the first hymn of praise in the Psalter and a meditation on Genesis 1. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is also Psalm 8.
readings: Psalm 8 is a poem on Genesis 1:26–28: humans are made like God and given rule over the creatures. Its question about human smallness under the stars has made it a favorite of scientists and poets; its answer is God's gift, not human greatness.
Read of the Son of Man

Hebrews 2:6–9 reads 8:4–6 of Jesus: humans do not yet rule all things, but Jesus, made lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory. Paul uses 8:6 of Christ's victory over every power (1 Corinthians 15:27). In this reading Psalm 8's human destiny is fulfilled in one man.

views.H: A hymn of David, perhaps from his years as a shepherd under the night sky (Jewish and Christian tradition). The Targum adds that the infants are those who praise God.
views.C: A hymn of creation from the monarchy or later, closely related to Genesis 1 (perhaps older than Genesis 1, perhaps drawing on it). It applies to humanity the royal language of the ancient Near East: every human is crowned like a king.
views.L: Psalm 8 is sung at feasts of Christ the King and of the Ascension in many churches, and verses of it are used in hymns of creation. The message of Pope Paul VI left on the moon by Apollo 11 in July 1969 was the text of Psalm 8.
views.J: The Talmud (Shabbat 88b) tells that when Moses went up to receive the Torah, the angels objected with 8:4 ('what is man?'), and Moses answered that the Torah's commands were meant for humans, not angels. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take elohim in 8:5 as angels.
views.X: The church fathers read 8:2 of the children who praised Jesus (Matthew 21:16) and the whole psalm of Christ. The Reformers read it as the dignity of human nature, now restored in Christ.

echoes: Genesis 1:26–28; Job 7:17–18; Psalm 144:3–4; Matthew 21:16; 1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22; Hebrews 2:6–9; Psalm 19:1

traditions.q: Can infants have faith? ('Out of the mouths of children and babies', 8:2)
views: Yes. Luther taught that God works faith in infants through baptism (Large Catechism, on baptism); Lutheran teachers point to Psalm 8:2 and Matthew 21:16 as showing that God draws praise from infants, so their faith is his work, not their reasoning.
Infants are baptized in the faith of the Church and receive grace, including the virtue of faith, as a gift; they do not yet make an act of faith of their own (Catechism 1250–1253).

Children of believers belong to the covenant and are baptized as such; God may regenerate infants, but the verse is not read as teaching that infants actively believe (Westminster Confession 28.4; 10.3).

Faith is a personal response that infants cannot yet make, so baptism waits for a profession of faith; the verse shows God can use the weakest voices, not that babies believe (Baptist Faith and Message, article 7).

settings.what: A hymn on God's glory and human dignity
settings.by: David, according to the title; one worshiper ('I see', 8:3) speaking for the congregation ('our Lord')
settings.when: At worship, perhaps at night or at a festival; the title's 'gittith' may point to the grape harvest
settings.why: To praise God's majesty and to marvel that the Creator gives small humans such honor and responsibility. Knowing it is sung to God, not lectured about him, keeps the human glory inside the frame of God's name.
settings.readers: For later Israel, often powerless among the nations, the psalm said that every human, not only kings, bears royal honor from God; the New Testament found that honor fulfilled in Jesus.

title: The Judge Who Remembers the Poor
sum: The psalmist thanks the LORD with all his heart for his wonders: enemies have turned back and perished, the nations are rebuked, their cities uprooted, their name erased. The LORD sits enthroned forever as judge of the world, a high tower for the downtrodden; he avenges blood and does not forget the cry of the afflicted. The nations have fallen into the pit they dug. The psalm ends with a plea: rise up, LORD, and let the nations learn they are only human.

Psalm 9 is the first half of an alphabet poem that continues in Psalm 10 (see 9:1): alef (9:1), bet (9:3), gimel (9:5), he (9:6), waw (9:7), zayin (9:11), chet (9:13), tet (9:15), yod (9:17) and kaf (9:18); dalet is missing or damaged. In the Greek and Latin numbering Psalms 9 and 10 are together Psalm 9, and from here the Greek numbers run one lower than the Hebrew.

views.H: A psalm of David, giving thanks for victories over the nations (2 Samuel 8). The Targum and Rashi read the title of Goliath's death, so that the psalm celebrates David's first great victory.
views.C: An acrostic thanksgiving and lament, joined with Psalm 10; many date it after the exile because acrostics are common in later poetry (Lamentations 1–4), though others think the form is old. It mixes the language of national victory with care for the poor.
views.L: Sung in the church's office as a psalm of God's justice; 9:9–10 is a common verse of comfort in Jewish and Christian prayer.
views.J: The Targum and Rashi link the title with Goliath (see 9:0). The psalm's alphabet form made it, like other acrostics, a text for memorizing.
views.X: Augustine read the title, in the Greek 'for the hidden things of the son', of the hidden judgment of Christ's first coming. The church has read the psalm as a promise that God will set the poor right at the last judgment.

echoes: Psalm 10; Psalm 7:15–16; Psalm 18:1–3; Psalm 46:1; Psalm 96:13; Genesis 9:5; Revelation 6:10

settings.what: A thanksgiving for God's judgment, ending in prayer
settings.by: David, according to the title; a worshiper who has seen God defeat enemies
settings.when: After a rescue or victory over foreign enemies; read with Psalm 10, also in a time of oppression at home
settings.why: To give thanks for God's past justice and to call the congregation to make it known, then to ask God to act again. It teaches that the God who judges nations is the high tower of the poor.
settings.readers: For Israel among the empires, the psalm said the nations were only human and the LORD remained on his throne; the acrostic form made it easy to learn by heart.

title: Why Do You Stand Far Off?
sum: The second half of the alphabet poem begins with a cry: why does the LORD stand far off in times of trouble? The wicked man, proud and greedy, hunts the poor like a lion, sets ambushes in the villages, and says to himself that God forgets and never looks. The psalmist calls on God to rise and lift his hand: God has seen, he takes trouble into his own hand, he is the orphan's helper. The LORD is king forever; he hears the humble and will give justice to the orphan and the oppressed so that no mortal will spread terror again.

The acrostic continues with lamed (10:1) and, after a middle (10:3–11) that has lost the pattern, ends with qof (10:12), resh (10:14), shin (10:15) and tav (10:17). Pe (10:7) and ayin (10:8) can be traced only if the word order is changed; the Greek and Romans 3:14 put "mouth" first in 10:7. Psalm 10 has no title. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is the second part of Psalm 9 (Greek 9:22–39).

views.H: Part of David's alphabet psalm with Psalm 9; traditional readers apply it to the oppressors of David's day or of any age.
views.C: A lament over social injustice inside Israel, joined to Psalm 9 by the acrostic. Its portrait of the wicked is close to the prophets (Micah 2:1–2; Amos 8:4–6).
views.L: Prayed by Christians and Jews as a psalm of the poor and of protest at God's seeming absence; 10:17–18 is used in prayers for justice.
views.J: Jewish prayer and commentary have taken up its 'why do you stand far off?' as Israel's question in times of persecution, and its picture of the wicked as a warning against those who say God does not see.
views.X: Paul quotes 10:7 in Romans 3:14. Liberation theologians and many others have read Psalm 10 as God's taking sides with the poor; Augustine read the wicked man as the Antichrist.

echoes: Psalm 9; Psalm 22:1; Psalm 14:1; Micah 2:1–2; Amos 8:4–6; Habakkuk 1:2–4; Romans 3:14; Psalm 146:9; James 5:1–6

settings.what: A lament over the oppression of the poor
settings.by: The psalmist of Psalm 9, continuing the alphabet poem; no title
settings.to: The LORD (10:1, 10:12–18), describing the wicked man to him (10:2–11)
settings.when: In a time when powerful men at home preyed on the poor and seemed to go unpunished
settings.why: To protest God's seeming absence, expose the practical atheism of the oppressor, and call on God the king to act for the orphan and the oppressed. It gives the powerless a voice in God's court.
settings.readers: Joined to Psalm 9, it taught Israel that the God who judges nations also judges the bullies of the village, and that complaint and praise belong in one prayer.

title: Fly to the Mountains?
sum: Friends urge the psalmist to flee like a bird to the hills: the wicked have their arrows on the string, and when society's foundations are being smashed, what can a righteous person do? He refuses. He has already found shelter in the LORD, who is in his holy temple and on his throne in heaven, whose eyes examine every human. The LORD tests the righteous, hates the lover of violence, and will rain judgment on the wicked like the fire and sulfur on Sodom. The upright will see his face.
Psalm 11 is a song of trust. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 10.

views.H: David's answer to advisers who urged him to flee from Saul (1 Samuel 19–23) or from Absalom.
views.C: A psalm of trust, perhaps of a temple refugee who has taken asylum in the sanctuary and refuses to leave it (11:1, 11:4); dated variously from the monarchy to after the exile.
views.L: In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer on Monday of the first week. It is used in prayers for courage under persecution.
views.J: Jewish commentators read the psalm of David hunted by Saul, and its 'foundations' as the pillars of justice or the righteous leaders on whom a people rests.
views.X: Christians have read it as a call to stand firm in persecution rather than flee from faithful witness, though most also allow that fleeing danger can be wise (Matthew 10:23).

echoes: 1 Samuel 23:14; 1 Samuel 26:20; Genesis 19:24; Habakkuk 2:20; Psalm 17:15; Psalm 27:4; Matthew 5:8; Revelation 22:4

settings.what: A song of trust under pressure to flee
settings.by: David, according to the title; a righteous person in danger
settings.to: The friends who urge flight (11:1–3), then the hearers, about the LORD (11:4–7)
settings.when: When advisers say the situation is hopeless and the only option is to run
settings.why: To refuse panic and flight by pointing to the LORD enthroned and watching. It gives courage to stay faithful when the foundations seem gone.
settings.readers: For Israel after the fall of Jerusalem, when the 'foundations' truly had been torn down, the psalm said the LORD's throne in heaven still stood.
views: Some scholars think the speaker had taken refuge in the sanctuary.
Others think of a king urged to abandon his city.

title: Pure Words in a Lying World
sum: The psalmist cries for help: the loyal have vanished, and everyone lies with smooth lips and a double heart, boasting that their tongues make them strong and no one is their master. Then the LORD speaks: because the poor are ruined and the needy groan, he will rise and set them in safety. His words, unlike human talk, are pure as silver refined seven times. He will guard his own, even while the wicked strut about.
Psalm 12 is a community lament with an oracle from God at its center. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 11.

views.H: A psalm of David at a time of widespread betrayal, such as Saul's court, where Doeg and the Ziphites informed on him (1 Samuel 22–23).
views.C: A communal lament with a prophetic oracle (12:5), probably used in temple worship; compare Micah 7:1–7 for the same complaint.
views.L: Sung in Lent and in times of public dishonesty; Luther's hymn Ach Gott vom Himmel sieh darein (1523) is a paraphrase of Psalm 12.
views.J: The rabbis read 12:6 ('pure words') of the Torah, refined and without dross; the Midrash on Psalms finds in 'seven times', seven times seven, the forty-nine ways a matter of Torah may be argued.
views.X: Christians have read 12:6 of the purity of Scripture. Luther's hymn on Psalm 12 became a Reformation lament over false teaching.

echoes: Micah 7:1–7; Isaiah 57:1; Psalm 18:30; Proverbs 30:5; Psalm 119:140; James 3:5–10

settings.what: A lament over a lying society, with God's answer
settings.by: David, according to the title; a voice for the faithful remnant; God speaks in 12:5
settings.to: The LORD (12:1, 12:7), with a report of the boasters' words (12:4) and the LORD's reply (12:5)
settings.when: In a time when lying and flattery are everywhere and the poor suffer from them
settings.why: To ask God to silence the liars, to hear his promise to rise for the oppressed, and to set his pure word against human deception.
settings.readers: Later Israel heard God's answer in 12:5 as a word for every generation of the poor, and the pure words of 12:6 as Scripture itself.

title: How Long?
sum: Four times the psalmist asks "How long?": how long will God forget him, hide his face, leave him wrestling with plans and grief, and let his enemy stand over him? He begs God to look and answer and brighten his eyes, before he sleeps the sleep of death and his enemies celebrate his fall. Then, with no change in his situation, he turns: he trusts in God's loyal love; his heart will be glad in God's rescue; he will sing, because the LORD has been generous to him.
Psalm 13 is the shortest complete lament in the Psalter and the model of the form. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 12.

views.H: A prayer of David in a long trial, perhaps the years of hiding from Saul.
views.C: The classic individual lament, with complaint, petition and vow of praise in six verses. Gunkel, Westermann and others use it to show the form.
views.L: Prayed widely in personal grief, depression and illness; it is among the psalms most used in pastoral care. Brahms set it for women's choir (Psalm 13, op. 27, 1859).
views.J: One midrash reads the four 'how longs' as the four kingdoms of Daniel, Babylon, Media, Greece and Rome, and the psalm as Israel's cry in exile.
views.X: The fathers read the psalm as the church's cry for Christ's return. Modern Christian writers on suffering use it to show that faith can say 'how long?' to God.

echoes: Psalm 6:3; Psalm 22:1–2; Psalm 44:24; Psalm 89:46; Habakkuk 1:2; Revelation 6:10; Daniel 12:2

settings.by: David, according to the title; one person who feels forgotten by God
settings.when: In a long trial, with illness or mortal danger (13:3) and a gloating enemy
settings.why: To give words to protest against God's seeming neglect, to ask for life, and to move from complaint to trust and a vow of praise. It shows that faith may speak both at once.
settings.readers: Israel in exile and the church in persecution prayed its 'how long?' as their own, with the confident ending as their hope.

title: The Fool Who Says There Is No God
sum: The fool says to himself that there is no God, and the whole human race has gone rotten: the LORD looks down from heaven for one wise person who seeks him, and finds none. Those who do wrong devour God's people as easily as bread. Yet terror falls on them, for God stands with the righteous, and the LORD is the poor man's shelter. The psalm ends with a longing for Israel's rescue to come out of Zion, when the LORD restores his people.
Psalm 14 appears again, with small changes, as Psalm 53 (see 14:2 and 14:5). In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 13.

deep.h: The same psalm twice: Psalms 14 and 53
deep.b:
Psalm 14 (Book I) and Psalm 53 (Book II) are one poem in two versions. The differences:

  • The name of God. 14 has YHWH, "the LORD," in 14:2, 14:4, 14:6 and 14:7; 53 has Elohim, "God," in the places matching 14:2, 14:4 and 14:7 (53:2, 53:4, 53:6), while 14:6 falls in the verse that 53 rewrites. Psalms 42–83 prefer Elohim throughout (the "Elohistic Psalter"), which most scholars explain as the work of an editor of that collection.
  • The title. 53 adds "on machalat" and "a maskil."
  • Small words. 14:1 "what they do" (alilah, deeds) is "injustice" (avel) in 53:1; 14:3 "turned aside" (sar) is "turned back" (sag) in 53:3.
  • 14:5–6 and 53:5. Here the two diverge most: 14 speaks of God with the righteous and the LORD as the poor man's shelter; 53 says "where no dread had been" and "God has scattered the bones of your besieger" (53:5).

Both versions were kept because each belonged to an older collection before the Psalter was joined. For readers today the pair is a window into how psalms were copied, adapted and reused. The Old Greek of 14:3 also carries six lines from Romans 3:13–18 (see the variant there).

views.H: A psalm of David; traditional Jewish readers (Rashi) take 14 as David foreseeing the first temple's destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, and 53 the second by Titus.
views.C: A prophetic lament or wisdom psalm, with 14:7 probably added in or after the exile. Psalms 14 and 53 show two lines of transmission for one text.
views.L: Verses 1–3 are quoted in sermons on sin, and 14:7 is sung in Advent as a prayer for salvation from Zion.
views.J: Rashi reads the two versions as two destructions of the temple.
views.X: Paul's use in Romans 3:10–12 made 14:1–3 a key text for the doctrine that all people are sinners in need of grace. Anselm began his ontological argument from the fool of 14:1.

echoes: Psalm 53; Psalm 10:4; Romans 3:10–12; Genesis 6:5; Genesis 11:5; Micah 3:1–3; Psalm 126:1–4

settings.what: A lament over human corruption, with a hope for Israel
settings.by: David, according to the title; a voice like a prophet's, speaking for God's people ('my people', 14:4)
settings.to: The hearers in general, about the fool and the LORD (14:1–6); then a wish for all Israel (14:7)
settings.when: In a time when the powerful oppress the poor and live as if God does not matter; 14:7 fits the exile
settings.why: To expose godless oppression as foolish, to assure the poor that God stands with them, and to long for God's rescue from Zion.
settings.readers: Exiles and their children heard 14:7 as the prayer for return; Paul made 14:1–3 a mirror for every human heart.

title: Who May Be the LORD's Guest?
sum: Who may stay as a guest in the LORD's tent, on his holy hill? The answer is a portrait: the wholehearted person who does right and speaks truth from the heart, who does not gossip, harm a neighbor or insult a friend, who rejects the wicked and honors those who fear the LORD, who keeps an oath even when it hurts, lends without interest, and refuses bribes. Such a person will never be toppled.
Psalm 15 is an entrance liturgy, a question and answer at the gate of the sanctuary. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 14.

views.H: David's psalm for the tent he set up for the ark on Zion (2 Samuel 6:17), teaching who may come near.
views.C: An entrance liturgy from the temple, comparable with Psalm 24:3–6 and Isaiah 33:14–16; the gatekeepers' 'torah' for pilgrims. Some see ten conditions, like the Ten Commandments.
views.L: Sung in Christian worship as a psalm of preparation; some churches use it before Communion.
views.J: The Talmud (Makkot 24a) says David reduced the 613 commandments to eleven in Psalm 15, Isaiah to six (Isaiah 33:15), Micah to three (Micah 6:8), Isaiah again to two, and Habakkuk to one: 'the righteous shall live by his faith' (Habakkuk 2:4).
views.X: Christian readers have asked how the psalm's conditions relate to grace: Luther and Calvin read them as the fruits of faith, the life of those already welcomed by God; others read them as the conduct Christ fulfilled.

echoes: Psalm 24:3–6; Isaiah 33:14–16; Micah 6:6–8; Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Matthew 5:8; Matthew 5:33–37

traditions.q: Does 'lends without charging interest' (15:5) forbid all interest on loans?
views: For centuries the Church forbade usury, any profit on a loan, citing this psalm and Luke 6:35 (Council of Vienne, 1311). Later teaching, recognizing money's productive use, allows moderate interest while condemning exploitative lending to the poor (Catechism 2269, 2449).
Calvin argued that the law forbade interest that oppresses the poor, not all interest on business loans; moderate interest is lawful if it is fair and the needy are lent to freely.
Luther condemned high interest and usury sharply in his sermons and tracts, while later Lutheran teaching accepted moderate interest under civil law.
Many Anabaptist and Mennonite communities practiced mutual aid and lent to members without interest, reading the psalm and Acts 4:32–35 as a pattern for the church.

settings.by: David, according to the title; in worship, worshipers ask (15:1) and a priest or gatekeeper answers (15:2–5)
settings.to: The LORD is asked (15:1); the answer is given to the worshipers at the gate
settings.when: As pilgrims arrived at the sanctuary on Zion for a festival
settings.why: To teach that the LORD's guests must live honestly and justly with their neighbors, in speech, money and court, not only bring sacrifices. The conditions bind every worshiper, rich or poor.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, gathered at the rebuilt temple, and for synagogue readers far from it, the psalm made the ethics of daily life the way into God's presence.

title: My Good Share
sum: The psalmist asks God to keep him, for God is his Lord and his only good. He delights in the holy ones of the land and refuses the drink offerings and names of other gods. The LORD is his share, his cup, his lot; his boundary lines have fallen in lovely places. He blesses the LORD who advises him, keeps him always before him, and will not be moved. So his heart is glad and his body rests secure, for God will not leave him to Sheol or let his loyal one see the Pit, but will show him the path of life and joy forever.
Psalm 16 is a song of trust. Peter and Paul quote 16:8–11 of Jesus' resurrection (Acts 2:25–31; Acts 13:35). In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 15.
readings: The language of share, lot and inheritance is the language of the land division, and the LORD as the portion of the Levites (Numbers 18:20). The psalmist, perhaps a priest or Levite, rejoices that his wealth is God himself, and expects God to keep him from an early death.

Acts 2 argues that David died and his body decayed, so 16:10 must speak of one who did not: Jesus, raised on the third day. Many Christians read the whole psalm as Christ's prayer; many Jewish and Christian readers also find in 16:10–11 the hope of life beyond death for the faithful.

views.H: A miktam of David, who trusted God to keep him alive among his enemies; Acts says he also spoke as a prophet of the Messiah (Acts 2:30–31).
views.C: A psalm of trust, perhaps of a convert from Canaanite worship (16:3–4) or of a Levite; the date is uncertain. Scholars debate whether 16:10–11 hopes for rescue from death now or for life after death.
views.L: Psalm 16 is sung at Easter and at funerals in many churches, and in the Roman rite at Night Prayer on Thursdays. Its 16:8 is the 'shiviti' of synagogue plaques.
views.J: Rashi reads 16:10 as David's prayer not to die for his sin, and Radak and Ibn Ezra of the soul's survival after death. The Talmud (Bava Batra 17a) cites 16:9, 'my flesh too will settle down in safety', for the view that worms had no power over David's body.
views.X: The church fathers read the psalm of Christ's death, descent and resurrection; 16:10 entered discussions of Christ's descent to the dead (1 Peter 3:19; the Apostles' Creed).

echoes: Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9; Psalm 73:23–26; Psalm 49:15; Acts 2:25–32; Acts 13:35–37; 1 Peter 3:18–20; Lamentations 3:24

traditions.q: Does 16:10, 'you will not leave my life to Sheol', teach that Christ descended to the dead?
views: Yes. Christ in his soul went down to the realm of the dead and freed the just who had gone before him, while his body did not decay; Acts 2:27 and the creed's 'he descended into hell' say this (Catechism 631–635).
Yes. Christ entered Hades as victor and broke its gates; the Easter icon of the Resurrection shows him pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs.
Yes. The whole Christ, body and soul, descended into hell after his burial to proclaim his victory over the devil and death, not to suffer (Formula of Concord, article 9).

The creed's descent is usually understood of Christ's suffering of God's wrath in soul on the cross and his remaining under the power of death until the third day (Heidelberg Catechism 44; Westminster Larger Catechism 50); the psalm's point is that his body did not decay.

Many evangelicals hold that Acts 2 uses the psalm only for the resurrection, and that the Bible does not teach a descent into hell; some, like Wayne Grudem, urge leaving the phrase out of the creed or explaining it as 'he was buried'.

settings.what: A song of trust and confession
settings.by: David, according to the title; a worshiper who has renounced other gods
settings.to: God (16:1–2, 16:5, 16:10–11); in 16:3–4 he speaks about the holy ones and the worshipers of other gods
settings.when: Unstated; perhaps a confession at the sanctuary by one who has chosen the LORD over other gods, or the prayer of a priest or Levite
settings.why: To declare the LORD his only good and his whole inheritance, and to express confidence that God will keep him from death. It teaches contentment and undivided loyalty.
settings.readers: Later Israel, living among other peoples' gods, prayed it as a vow of loyalty; the first Christians found in 16:10 the promise kept in Jesus' resurrection.
views: Kraus and others: God will keep him from an early death.
Dahood, many Jewish medieval and Christian readers: a hope of unending life with God.

title: The Shadow of Your Wings
sum: An innocent man brings his case to God: let your verdict come from you; you have tested me by night and found nothing; I have kept to your paths. He asks God to show the wonders of his loyal love, to guard him like the pupil of the eye and hide him under his wings from enemies who have hardened their hearts and track him like a lion. He calls on the LORD to rise and bring them down, men whose only share is in this life. As for him, he will see God's face and be satisfied when he wakes.
Psalm 17 is a prayer of the falsely accused, like Psalm 7. In the Greek and Latin numbering it is Psalm 16.

views.H: A prayer of David pursued by Saul in the wilderness of Maon, when Saul's men closed in around him (1 Samuel 23:25–28).
views.C: An individual lament of an accused person, perhaps spending the night in the temple and awaiting God's verdict in the morning (17:3, 17:15).
views.L: Sung at Compline in some traditions because of 17:8 ('hide me in the shade of your wings'), a common night prayer in Christian and Jewish use. The Roman Compline versicle 'Keep us as the apple of your eye; hide us in the shadow of your wings' comes from it.
views.J: The rabbis read 17:15 ('I will see your face in righteousness') as teaching that giving charity (tsedaqah) opens the way to see God (Bavli Bava Batra 10a). 17:8 appears in the bedtime prayers.
views.X: The fathers read 17:15 of the resurrection and the vision of God; Jerome's Gallican Psalter 'when your glory appears' was read of the second coming.

echoes: Psalm 7:3–9; Psalm 26:1–3; Deuteronomy 32:10–11; Ruth 2:12; Psalm 36:7; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 91:4; Matthew 23:37; Psalm 11:7; 1 John 3:2

settings.what: A prayer for vindication and protection
settings.by: David, according to the title; a person falsely accused and hunted
settings.when: When enemies surround him; many think during a night in the sanctuary, awaiting God's judgment by morning
settings.why: To appeal to God's verdict, ask for his protection like a mother bird's, and set the enemies' satisfaction with this world against his own satisfaction in God. It teaches the accused to wait for God's judgment.
settings.readers: Later worshipers prayed its night images as a bedtime prayer, and its last verse as the hope of seeing God, on waking from sleep or from death.
